drink:Champagne — grower fizz (the close.name: Champagne, grower bottles
drink:Champagne — grower fizz (the close.teaser: Two small letters near the cork, RM, tell you one family grew the grapes and made the wine
drink:Champagne — grower fizz (the close.story: The big Champagne houses buy grapes from hundreds of growers across the region and blend them into a house style that tastes the same every year. A récoltant-manipulant does the opposite: one family farms its own vines, often in a single village, and makes and bottles the wine itself. The code is printed in small type on the label, usually near the bottom: RM for a grower, NM for a négociant house, CM for a cooperative. Champagne is the nearest serious vineyard to Paris, a short train ride east from the Gare de l'Est, so a grower bottle is about as local as the city's wine gets.
drink:Champagne — grower fizz (the close.why: Ask what grower fizz they have open by the glass; a good wine bar usually has one, and it is rarely dearer than the house brand.
facts: Finer, more precise bubbles than the brand-name blends; chalk, bread and green apple, with the village showing through
RM in the small print near the bottom; brut nature or extra brut means little or no added sugar
Une coupe de champagne de vigneron. Names to look for: Chartogne-Taillet, Pierre Péters, Larmandier-Bernier, Egly-Ouriet, Vouette et Sorbée

drink:Chablis & Sancerre — the two bistr.name: Chablis & Sancerre
drink:Chablis & Sancerre — the two bistr.teaser: Order un verre de blanc and you will usually be offered one of these two: ancient seabed or Loire flint
drink:Chablis & Sancerre — the two bistr.story: Most bistro white lists open with these two. Chablis is chardonnay from the far north of Burgundy, grown on Kimmeridgian marl, a seabed some 150 million years old still packed with tiny fossil oysters; in its plain village form it is made without new oak, so it tastes of lemon and wet stone rather than butter. Sancerre is sauvignon blanc from the upper Loire. On its flint soils it gives a struck-match, gunsmoke smell the French call pierre à fusil. Either one should taste sharp and saline. Vanilla or toast on the nose means it is not the classic style. The Chablis vineyards belong to the Burgundy guide.
drink:Chablis & Sancerre — the two bistr.why: With oysters or a plate of charcuterie, ask for either one by name instead of house white; the jump in quality costs a few euros.
facts: Chablis: lemon, oyster shell, chalk. Sancerre: grapefruit, cut grass, flint smoke
Chablis, Chablis Premier Cru or Grand Cru (Petit Chablis is the lighter outer ring); Sancerre names its village or lieu-dit on the better bottles

Un verre de Chablis or un Sancerre blanc. Growers to look for: Raveneau, Vincent Dauvissat, Louis Michel, William Fèvre for Chablis; Vacheron, Alphonse Mellot, François Cotat, Gérard Boulay for Sancerre

drink:Beaujolais — the natural, chilled.name: Beaujolais crus
drink:Beaujolais — the natural, chilled.teaser: Not the November nouveau: cru gamay from Morgon or Fleurie, low on sulphur and served cool
drink:Beaujolais — the natural, chilled.story: Beaujolais has two lives. One is the nouveau, rushed out every November. The other is the ten crus, villages like Morgon, Fleurie and Chiroubles, whose granite slopes give gamay real depth. In the 1980s a handful of Morgon growers took advice from the chemist and négociant Jules Chauvet and began making wine with whole bunches, native yeasts and little or no added sulphur. Marcel Lapierre, Jean Foillard, Jean-Paul Thévenet and Guy Breton became known as the Gang of Four, and many trace the natural-wine movement back to them. Their wines are what Paris's natural-wine counters pour most; those rooms have their own cards below.
drink:Beaujolais — the natural, chilled.why: Ask for it slightly cool, about twenty minutes in the fridge; the fruit tightens and it drinks like a cold glass of cherries.
facts: Light to mid red, crushed cherry and raspberry, a peppery lift; little tannin
The cru name (Morgon, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Moulin-à-Vent) rather than plain Beaujolais; 'sans soufre ajouté' if no sulphur was added
Un Morgon, un peu frais. Growers: Lapierre, Foillard, Thévenet, Guy Breton, Yvon Métras, Georges Descombes, Jean-Claude Lapalu

drink:Cidre & Poiré — the honest outside.name: Cidre & poiré
drink:Cidre & Poiré — the honest outside.teaser: Not Paris at all: Normandy and Brittany in a bottle, made to sit next to a buckwheat galette
drink:Cidre & Poiré — the honest outside.story: Paris grows no apples to speak of; cider here is a visitor from Normandy and Brittany, and it belongs at the crêperie table with a buckwheat galette. The best of it drinks more like wine than beer. Eric Bordelet, who was a sommelier at L'Arpège before going home to his family orchards in the Domfrontais, on the Normandy–Mayenne border, makes cider and perry that ferment slowly and finish their sparkle in the bottle. Poiré is the pear version, paler and more floral. Look for brut on the label if you want it dry. Breizh Café and La Crêperie de Josselin have their own cards in the tables.
drink:Cidre & Poiré — the honest outside.why: Order a brut cider in a bolée, the wide ceramic cup, with a complète galette; that is the pairing it was made for.
facts: Cloudy to clear gold, baked apple or pear, fine bubbles; brut is dry, doux is sweet
Cidre or poiré; brut or doux; Cidre de Cornouaille AOP for Brittany, Domfrontais for pear perry
Une bolée de cidre brut, or a bottle of Bordelet Sydre or Poiré; also Cyril Zangs

drink:Pastis — the Marseille drink Paris.name: Pastis
drink:Pastis — the Marseille drink Paris.teaser: An anise drink from Marseille, poured on every Paris terrasse, that turns milky the moment water hits it
drink:Pastis — the Marseille drink Paris.story: Pastis is not Parisian; it comes from Provence and the Marseille waterfront, but every zinc bar in the city keeps a bottle. It arrives as a short measure of amber spirit with a carafe of cold water beside it. Add about five parts water to one of pastis and the glass clouds over: the anise oils fall out of solution as the alcohol is diluted, an effect called the louche. A footnote for the curious: Paris has a licensed still again, the Distillerie de Paris, opened in 2015 and billed as the first in the city since 1914, though it makes gin, whisky and rum, not pastis.
drink:Pastis — the Marseille drink Paris.why: Pour the water yourself, slowly, and add ice only after; bartenders say ice first dulls the anise.
facts: Cloudy pale yellow, liquorice, fennel and herbs; served long with water
Ricard and Pastis 51 are the café defaults (both Pernod Ricard); Henri Bardouin, from Forcalquier in Provence, is the craft bottle, made with up to 65 plants and spices, 45%
Un pastis, or ask whether they have Henri Bardouin; a Ricard is the same order as 'un jaune'

drink:Café crème — the breakfast-only mi.name: Café crème
drink:Café crème — the breakfast-only mi.teaser: The big milky coffee is for breakfast; after lunch, Paris switches to a short black or a noisette
drink:Café crème — the breakfast-only mi.story: Un crème is an espresso topped up with hot milk in a large cup, and Parisians drink it in the morning, with a croissant, often standing at the counter. Order one after lunch and the waiter will place you as a visitor before you open your mouth. From noon the order is un express, a plain short coffee, or un noisette, an espresso with a dash of milk, named for its hazelnut colour. It is not a cappuccino: there is no foam art, and plant milk is mostly found in the newer specialty coffee bars, which have their own cards.
drink:Café crème — the breakfast-only mi.why: Say 'un crème' rather than 'a coffee with milk', and drink it before eleven; the half-second of French is the whole trick.
facts: Espresso and steamed milk in a big cup, little foam
Nothing to read: in a classic café the coffee is the house blend
Un crème in the morning; un express or un noisette after lunch

natural-wine:Le Verre Vole.name: Le Verre Volé
natural-wine:Le Verre Vole.teaser: A wine shop with a kitchen on the canal: pick a bottle off the shelf and eat what the chef built around it
natural-wine:Le Verre Vole.story: Cyril Bordarier opened Le Verre Volé in 2000 near the Canal Saint-Martin, and it was one of the very first caves à manger, a bottle shop where you can also sit down and eat. The walls are the wine list: some 400 natural references on the shelves, and you choose by looking, asking and pointing. The kitchen, run by chef Takao Inazawa, sends out short plates meant to flatter what is in the glass. The room is about the size of a large living room, so tables are close and conversation crosses them. A quarter-century on, much of the city's natural-wine scene follows the format it set.
natural-wine:Le Verre Vole.why: Ask the staff to pick a bottle around one dish and one budget; that conversation is why people come.
facts: 67 rue de Lancry, 10th, by the Canal Saint-Martin
Natural wine from the shelves, some 400 references, with short seasonal plates
Book for dinner; listings disagree on hours (lunch and dinner most days, Oct 2026), so check when you reserve

natural-wine:La Buvette.name: La Buvette
natural-wine:La Buvette.teaser: A former dairy shop on rue Saint-Maur with a few tables, a zinc bar and small plates out of jars and tins
natural-wine:La Buvette.story: Camille Fourmont opened La Buvette in December 2012 in what had been a small crémerie, after working at Inaki Aizpitarte's Le Dauphin. There are only a few tables and a zinc counter. The food is assembled rather than cooked: giant white beans dressed in oil, slices of cédrat citron, marinated small fish or octopus, good bread. The short wine list is natural, and you can pull a bottle from the shelf and drink it on the spot for a small corkage. Fourmont later wrote the recipe-and-wine book that carries the bar's name. There are no reservations.
natural-wine:La Buvette.why: Order the white beans with whatever she is pouring by the glass; it is the plate everyone writes about.
facts: A short natural list by the glass; shelf bottles to drink in for a small corkage
Right at opening, early evening; no bookings and very few seats

natural-wine:Septime La Cave.name: Septime La Cave
natural-wine:Septime La Cave.teaser: Septime's bottle shop and bar: stand at the counter or on the pavement, cult growers, sharp snacks
natural-wine:Septime La Cave.story: A few steps from Septime, the restaurant that has its own card, La Cave is a small bottle shop that turns into a standing bar in the afternoon. There are almost no seats; on a fine evening the drinkers spill onto rue Basfroi. The list changes fast and leans on low-intervention growers, a lot of Jura, Rhône and grower Champagne, with snacks to match: cheese, charcuterie, a tin of fish. Because it takes no bookings it is also the easiest way to taste the Septime team's choices without a table next door.
natural-wine:Septime La Cave.why: Come straight after work, before the counter fills, and ask what was opened today.
facts: A fast-rotating natural list by the glass and bottle, Jura, Rhône and grower Champagne heavy
Around 18:00, before the pavement crowd; no bookings, listed daily 16:00–23:00 (Oct 2026, listings vary)

rooftops:The rooftop terrace, Galeries L.name: Galeries Lafayette terrace
rooftops:The rooftop terrace, Galeries L.teaser: Eighth floor above the 1912 glass dome: Opéra, Sacré-Cœur and the Eiffel Tower, no ticket
rooftops:The rooftop terrace, Galeries L.story: Take the escalators to the top of the Coupole building and you come out onto an open terrace above the department store's famous glass-and-steel dome. Below you is the green copper roof of the Palais Garnier; turn and Sacré-Cœur sits on its hill to the north, the Eiffel Tower to the south-west. Nobody checks a ticket and there is no queue to pay. Since May 2026 the rooftop restaurant has been Balcon, a classic bistro from chef Julien Sebbag, which replaced the vegetarian Créatures. The terrace keeps shop hours, so this is a daylight view rather than a sunset drink.
rooftops:The rooftop terrace, Galeries L.why: Go on a clear morning on a weekday, when you can have the Opéra rail almost to yourself.
facts: 8th floor, Coupole building, Galeries Lafayette Haussmann, 9th
Balcon, Julien Sebbag's bistro, for a drink or a meal; the terrace itself needs no order
Terrace free (Oct 2026); open Mon–Sat 10:00–19:30, Sun and holidays 11:00–19:30; Balcon's winter hours not yet published, check
Weekday mornings; in winter, an hour before the 19:30 close

rooftops:Le Perchoir Ménilmontant.name: Le Perchoir Ménilmontant
rooftops:Le Perchoir Ménilmontant.teaser: Seven floors up in the working east, looking west over the roofs of the Paris the postcards skip
rooftops:Le Perchoir Ménilmontant.story: Le Perchoir is the bar most often credited with starting the Paris rooftop habit, and it sits on top of an old industrial building in Ménilmontant rather than a palace hotel. The bar is open to the sky, a level above the restaurant, with the zinc roofs and chimney pots of the 11th and 20th rolling west towards the domes of the centre. After dark it is loud and packed, not the place for a quiet aperitif. Its sibling on top of the BHV in the Marais has closed; this original is the one still pouring.
rooftops:Le Perchoir Ménilmontant.why: Arrive for the last hour of daylight and stay at the rail; the view runs right across the city to the west.
facts: Ménilmontant, 11th, on the top floor above the restaurant
Cocktails, wine and beer at the roof bar; the restaurant floor below works year-round

Cocktails about EUR 14–18 (Oct 2026); listed Mon–Fri 18:00–02:00, Sat 16:00–02:00, Sun 16:00–00:00. The open roof is seasonal, at its best late spring to early autumn, with a heated covered area in winter; check before going

rooftops:Le Tout-Paris.name: Le Tout-Paris
rooftops:Le Tout-Paris.teaser: Seventh floor of the Cheval Blanc at the Pont Neuf, the Seine laid out from Notre-Dame to the Eiffel Tower
rooftops:Le Tout-Paris.story: The Cheval Blanc hotel fills part of the old Samaritaine department store at the Pont Neuf, and Le Tout-Paris is its seventh-floor brasserie, done up in loud colour by the designer Peter Marino. From the terrace the Seine runs both ways: Notre-Dame upstream, the Louvre and the Eiffel Tower downstream. William Bequin cooks under the direction of Arnaud Donckele, and the brasserie won a Michelin star in March 2024, which it still holds. This is the expensive end of the city's rooftops, but the long marble bar takes walk-ins, so one drink at the counter buys the same view as dinner.
rooftops:Le Tout-Paris.why: Skip dinner and take one cocktail at the marble bar, facing the Pont Neuf.
facts: 7th floor, Cheval Blanc Paris, by the Pont Neuf, 1st
Cocktails at the marble bar; Michelin-starred brasserie cooking at the tables
Splurge tier; bar open daily 07:00–01:00, walk-in only; restaurant booked by phone or email (Oct 2026)
Late afternoon, before the dinner service fills the terrace

hotel-bars:Bar Hemingway, Ritz Paris.name: Bar Hemingway
hotel-bars:Bar Hemingway, Ritz Paris.teaser: Twenty-odd seats, wood panels and the writer's photographs, at the back of the Ritz on the place Vendôme
hotel-bars:Bar Hemingway, Ritz Paris.story: The little bar at the back of the Ritz has been pouring since 1921, under names that included Le Petit Bar, before it took Hemingway's. The name comes from a story he liked to tell: that in August 1944 he 'liberated' the Ritz and ran up a tab for fifty-one dry martinis. Nobody can prove the count. The bar went dark in 1982 and stayed shut twelve years, until Colin Field reopened it in 1994 and made it famous for drinks mixed to the guest rather than a menu. Field left in June 2023 after nearly three decades; his successors keep the room, the panelling and the photographs.
hotel-bars:Bar Hemingway, Ritz Paris.why: Get there before it opens and take a seat at the counter; once the twenty-five or so places are gone, you wait outside.
facts: Classic cocktails, the dry martini above all
Cocktails about EUR 32–34 (Oct 2026); evenings from about 17:00 to midnight, days vary by listing; smart dress
At opening; listings disagree on whether it books, so ask the hotel

hotel-bars:Le Bar du Bristol.name: Le Bar du Bristol
hotel-bars:Le Bar du Bristol.teaser: A collector's study of a bar on the Faubourg Saint-Honoré, with a DJ after ten at the end of the week
hotel-bars:Le Bar du Bristol.story: Le Bristol opened in April 1925 on the rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré, the street of the Élysée Palace, and its regulars have always been diplomats and fashion people. The bar is much younger: it opened in 2012, styled as a cabinet of curiosities, low-lit, full of objects, with contemporary video art playing behind the counter. Cocktails arrive with small bites, and the Bristol Old Fashioned is the house signature. What sets it apart from other palace bars is the late shift: on Bristol After Dark nights a DJ takes over and the hush gives way to a party.
hotel-bars:Le Bar du Bristol.why: Come on a Thursday to Saturday after ten for After Dark, or at five for the quiet version.
facts: Le Bristol, 112 rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré, 8th (Miromesnil)
Signature cocktails, the Bristol Old Fashioned first, with small bites

hotel-bars:Bar Joséphine, Hôtel Lutetia.name: Bar Joséphine
hotel-bars:Bar Joséphine, Hôtel Lutetia.teaser: Frescoes from 1910 found under layers of paint, and live music under them three nights a week
hotel-bars:Bar Joséphine, Hôtel Lutetia.story: The Lutetia opened in 1910, built by the family behind Le Bon Marché to lodge the store's grand customers, and it was the first luxury hotel on the Left Bank; Picasso, Joyce and Saint-Exupéry all passed through. During the 2014–2018 restoration, workers found the bar's original ceiling and wall frescoes by Adrien Karbowsky hidden under coats of paint and white-painted glass, and some 17,000 hours went into bringing them back. The bar is named for Josephine Baker. In 2019 the hotel received France's Palace distinction, and it now runs under Mandarin Oriental.
hotel-bars:Bar Joséphine, Hôtel Lutetia.why: Time it for a live set, Thursday to Saturday, and sit where you can look up at the ceiling.
facts: Cocktails and Champagne, with live music
Open 17:00–01:00; live music Thu–Sat 20:00–23:00, paused 5 July–9 September (hotel page, seen Oct 2026)
A Thursday to Saturday from about 20:00

listening:Bambino.name: Bambino
listening:Bambino.teaser: Dinner to records collected in Japan, then the tables fold away and the room becomes a dance floor
listening:Bambino.story: Fabien Lombardi opened Bambino in 2019 on rue Saint-Sébastien, borrowing the idea of the Japanese music bar, where the sound system matters as much as the menu. Raw concrete, shelves of records and oversized speakers fill the room, and Lombardi has said most of the vinyl was bought on trips to Japan. Early in the evening it is a restaurant, with natural wine and small plates; later the tables are cleared and funk, disco and soul pull a crowd onto the floor, especially at weekends. It is a dinner place that turns into a party, not a hushed listening room.
listening:Bambino.why: Book a late dinner seating so you are still there when the tables go and the volume comes up.
facts: Natural wine and cocktails, funk, disco and soul on vinyl
Open daily from early evening to about 02:00 (hours vary by listing, Oct 2026)
After 23:00, when the dining room becomes a dance floor

listening:Notre Dame Music Bar.name: Notre Dame Music Bar
listening:Notre Dame Music Bar.teaser: Whole albums played side to side on tube amps, in a small room where you lower your voice
listening:Notre Dame Music Bar.story: Japan's jazz kissa are small cafés where people come to listen to records on a serious system, and Notre Dame Music Bar brings the idea to a side street in the 11th. Albums are played through, start to finish, under low light. Vintage McIntosh valve amplifiers drive JBL speakers, and some two thousand records line the walls. The room holds about sixty, the wine and snacks are chosen with care, and the house rule is simple: talk quietly, the music comes first. There are no reservations.
listening:Notre Dame Music Bar.why: Ask what is on the turntable and let the side finish before you order another glass.
facts: Jazz and other albums on vinyl, played whole; wine and small plates
No bookings; listed Mon–Wed 18:00–23:30, Thu–Sat 18:00–01:00 (2025 listing, seen Oct 2026)
Early on a weekday, when the room is quiet enough to hear everything

listening:Caveau de la Huchette.name: Caveau de la Huchette
listening:Caveau de la Huchette.teaser: Down the stairs into a medieval vault where swing bands have played almost nightly since the 1940s
listening:Caveau de la Huchette.story: On a narrow street of cheap restaurants by Saint-Michel, a staircase leads down into stone vaults several centuries old. Jazz arrived after the war, in 1946 by most accounts, and the cellar has had live bands nearly every night since: Sidney Bechet, Lionel Hampton, Count Basie and Art Blakey all played here. The vibraphonist Dany Doriz, a friend of Hampton's, has owned it since 1970, and the music still leans towards swing, boogie and blues. The floor is narrow and the dancers are serious. Older stories of Rosicrucians and a Revolution-era 'cellar of terror' are legend.
listening:Caveau de la Huchette.why: Go down even if you do not dance; watching the regulars swing out under the vault is the show.
facts: Rue de la Huchette, Latin Quarter, 5th (Saint-Michel)
Live swing, boogie-woogie and blues bands, with dancing, every night

listening:Duc des Lombards.name: Duc des Lombards
listening:Duc des Lombards.teaser: Two sets a night, six nights a week, in a small club where the band is a few metres away
listening:Duc des Lombards.story: On rue des Lombards, a short walk from Châtelet, the Duc des Lombards is a jazz club built for listening: a small room, the band close, and an audience that keeps quiet while it plays. The programme mixes French and visiting players, from established names to young groups, in two sets an evening, with cheaper nights given to younger groups. At the end of the week the music runs on after midnight with a free jam session, when local musicians drop in after their own gigs.
listening:Duc des Lombards.why: Book the early set to hear the band fresh, or turn up after midnight on Friday or Saturday for the free jam.
facts: Live jazz, two sets a night Monday to Saturday; free jam Friday and Saturday from midnight

listening:New Morning.name: New Morning
listening:New Morning.teaser: Opened in 1981 with Art Blakey on stage; jazz, soul and world music for a few hundred standing
listening:New Morning.story: Eglal Farhi, born in Egypt in 1922, was nearly sixty when she opened New Morning in what had been a printing works on rue des Petites-Écuries. The first concert, on 16 April 1981, was Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers. Over the next decades Dizzy Gillespie, Chet Baker and Prince played here, and the programme widened to soul, blues, Brazilian and African music. Farhi's daughter Catherine has run the club since 2010; Eglal died in 2019. It holds a few hundred people, so even big names play close enough to see their hands.
listening:New Morning.why: Check the listings a few weeks ahead; international acts here sell out, and the room is small for who plays it.
facts: Concerts most nights: jazz, soul, world and Latin; some seated, many standing
Tickets about EUR 28–35 for autumn 2026 shows (Oct 2026)

listening:La Recyclerie.name: La Recyclerie
listening:La Recyclerie.teaser: A disused railway station at Porte de Clignancourt, now a canteen, a bar and a farm on the old tracks
listening:La Recyclerie.story: The Gare Ornano was a stop on the Petite Ceinture, the ring railway that once circled Paris inside the walls and lost its passengers long ago. Since 2014 the station has been La Recyclerie, a 'third place' that mixes a café-canteen with an urban farm of about a thousand square metres strung along the abandoned rails. Around that run repair workshops, documentary nights and weekend markets, and the benches fill with families, students and neighbourhood regulars. From late 2026 the old station hosts a free winter village through the holidays.
listening:La Recyclerie.why: Take your coffee out to the platform terrace and look down the tracks; the line still runs off into the green.
facts: Former Gare Ornano, Porte de Clignancourt, 18th (metro line 4)
Coffee, beer, wine and canteen plates, plus talks, workshops and markets

listening:Ground Control.name: Ground Control
listening:Ground Control.teaser: An SNCF hall of some 6,500 square metres by the Gare de Lyon, turned into food stalls, bars and workshops
listening:Ground Control.story: Behind the Gare de Lyon, the Halle Charolais was a railway postal-sorting hall before Ground Control took it over in 2017. Now its 6,500 or so square metres hold a string of food counters from many kitchens, bars, a bookshop and makers' stalls, galleries and a rolling calendar of talks, quiz nights, concerts and children's parties. The long tables pull in a mix you rarely see in one room in Paris: office workers, families, students and railway staff. In February 2026 it added a small Nordic bathing space.
listening:Ground Control.why: Come for a weekend lunch, pick from several counters, and stay for whatever is on in the hall that afternoon.
facts: Halle Charolais, rue du Charolais, 12th, behind the Gare de Lyon
Street food from many counters, craft beer, wine and cocktails, with events most weeks

listening:La Station - Gare des Mines.name: La Station – Gare des Mines
listening:La Station - Gare des Mines.teaser: An old coal station at Porte d'Aubervilliers, home to experimental nights, until it closes on 31 October 2026
listening:La Station - Gare des Mines.story: Out at the ring road, on the site of a former coal station, Collectif MU built a music yard that does what the centre cannot: post-punk and EBM gigs, organic house and late techno, cheap drinks, open air, and the Garage MU festival. In April 2026 the collective announced it would close for about three years from 31 October 2026 while the site is rebuilt as part of the new Porte d'Aubervilliers quarter, where the city has promised it a place. The closing party is on the last night of October. It earns some 85 percent of its own money and has asked for donations to get through.

listening:Chanson, the caves and the Fre.name: Chanson, caves and the French touch
listening:Chanson, the caves and the Fre.teaser: From Piaf and the Saint-Germain cellars to Daft Punk and Ed Banger: the three ways Paris sounds
listening:Chanson, the caves and the Fre.story: Paris sings first in chanson: Édith Piaf, then Jacques Brel, Georges Brassens, Léo Ferré and Serge Gainsbourg, who all worked the post-war cafés and cabarets of Saint-Germain. In the late 1940s the quarter's cellars became jazz caves; at Le Tabou on rue Dauphine, Boris Vian played trumpet and the existentialist crowd danced underground. The city's modern export is electronic. In the 1990s the 'French touch' of Daft Punk filtered disco through house, and in 2003 Pedro Winter, then Daft Punk's manager, founded Ed Banger Records, home to Justice, SebastiAn and DJ Mehdi. Gainsbourg's house on rue de Verneuil, covered in graffiti, opened to visitors in 2023.
listening:Chanson, the caves and the Fre.why: Book the Maison Gainsbourg weeks ahead, then walk to rue Dauphine, where the Tabou cellar stood.
facts: Maison Gainsbourg: the house at 5 bis and the museum at 14 rue de Verneuil, 7th; booking essential, closed Mondays, house and museum about EUR 29–32 (listings conflict, Oct 2026). For live swing in a cellar of that era, the Caveau de la Huchette has its own card

Whether Miles Davis actually sat in at Le Tabou during his 1949 Paris visit, or only passed through the Saint-Germain clubs, is told both ways; and who first used 'French touch' for the Paris house sound is disputed

_notes: Searched 18 times (standard). Biggest correction: Colin Field left Bar Hemingway in June 2023; the old card said he was still there in 2026. La Station - Gare des Mines closes after 31 October 2026 for about three years: the card says so and must be pulled or rewritten after that date. Hours for Le Verre Volé, Septime La Cave, Bambino, Bar Hemingway and the Bristol After Dark nights conflict between listings; the cards say 'check'. Notre Dame Music Bar hours come from a 2025 blog. Caveau de la Huchette prices are from an undated Paris je t'aime page; its jazz start is 1946 or 1949 depending on the source. La Buvette was not re-verified (no search result) and has no street number. Sites given only where the domain is the venue's own (verrevole.com, labuvette.paris, septime-lacave.fr, Galeries Lafayette, chevalblanc.com, oetkerhotels.com for Le Bristol, mandarinoriental.com for the Lutetia, caveaudelahuchette.fr, ducdeslombards.com, newmorning.com, larecyclerie.com, groundcontrolparis.com, lastation.paris, maisongainsbourg.fr); the last few are named by listings or old sources but were not opened (WebFetch unavailable).
